items.title: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on Vera Rubin NVL72: 58x Throughput vs. GB300 NVL72 at 387 tokens/s
items.summary: On one NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, vLLM serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on SemiAnalysis AgentX at 1.7M tokens/s per GPU at a P90 of 387 tokens/s per user, 58x GB300 NVL72 at the same interactivity.

items.content_excerpt: TL;DR: On one NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, vLLM serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 1.7M tokens/s per GPU while each user gets 387 tokens/s, 58× GB300 NVL72, and reaches 2.52M at peak throughput and 1,810 tokens/s for a single user. The gains come from building on what is new in Rubin: kernels tuned for its split memory and FP4 tensor cores, specialized decode kernels for low latency, and a rack-wide KV cache and Engram tables shared over NVLink. This is the third post in our DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash series. The first post covered day-0 bring-up and kernel fusions. The second scaled the model to a GB300 NVL72 rack with P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP. This post moves the same stack to Vera Rubin NVL72, which we introduced last month . Rubin opens up new avenues for optimization. We start with the hardware facts that shaped our work, then go through four groups of optimizations: Figure 1: SemiAnalysis AgentX on NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 (vLLM, P/D disaggregation, Wide-EP) vs. GB300 NVL72. Throughput counts cached input, uncached input and output tokens ( GB300 source ). We measure performance with the SemiAnalysis AgentX benchmark as a representative agentic serving workload, aligned with our previous posts. Figure 1 compares the two racks' raw throughput (total tokens per GPU per second, including input, cached, and output) and power-normalized throughput, respectively in two tabs. We use the same methodology as in our previous GB300 post . For kernels and model forward profiling, vllm bench forward times exact prefill and decode batches through the real execute_model path, with real weights and real AgentX tokens. We A/B prefill kernels in loops that run for several seconds and report sustained numbers where they differ. Three properties of Vera Rubin NVL72 drove most of the decisions below. Where an optimization is specific to Rubin, we say which of them it relies on. Figure 2: Weight stages of the routed-expert GEMM in one SM's shared memory, with the SM100 MXFP8×MXFP4 MMA and with SM107's K64 MXFP8×MXFP4 MMA on packed FP4. We kept GB300's three engine shapes: DEP2 prefill, Wide-EP decode (DEP16 or DEP32), and a TP decode path for the lowest latency (next section). We also kept DeepSeek's kernel set (MegaMoE, MegaAttn, Mega-mHC, MegaGate, DeepSelect) and rebuilt much of it for SM107. items.title: JioHotstar Benchmarks Knowledge Bases for AI Coding Agents
items.summary:
JioHotstar evaluated 6 approaches to code retrieval for AI coding agents using SWE, CodeScale Bench, and an internal question-answering harness. Structural search performed well on concrete tasks, while semantic retrieval helped with ambiguous requirements. The findings highlight trade-offs in accuracy, token use, and tool design, underscoring the need to match retrieval tools to task types.

items.title: Inkling 2 Small on vLLM: Day-0 Support
items.summary: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small from day 0: attention residuals, a new decode kernel for relative-bias attention, all-reduce fused with the ops around it, and DSpark speculative decoding.
items.story_key: model:vllm|variant:small|title:inkling 2 small on vllm day 0 support
items.content_excerpt: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small on day 0. It is a multimodal (text and vision) MoE model with 594B total and 17B active parameters and up to 1M tokens of context. The model also comes with a native DSpark speculator. vLLM supports it with optimized performance (up to 630 TPS/user at TP4 and acceptance length 3.5) and also supports LoRA. Figure 1. Inkling 2 Small architecture. Gold marks what is new or changed since Inkling. Inkling backbone + recent advances. Inkling 2 Small keeps Inkling's backbone: the 5:1 mix of sliding-window and full attention, GQA with a learned relative bias instead of RoPE, the four short convolutions per layer and a sigmoid-routed MoE. On top of it, it adds recent advances. Block attention residuals replace the residual stream, so before each sublayer a learned query mixes the outputs of earlier 6-layer blocks. Gated attention puts a sigmoid gate on each head's output, together with a per-token attention sink . It replaces the hMLP image encoder with a 23-layer ViT. Mixed-precision MoE with Four-Over-Six NVFP4. Out of Inkling 2 Small's 48 layers, the experts of the first 40 use NVFP4 and those of the last 8 use MXFP8. The NVFP4 activations use a per-token global scale plus dual-candidate block scales ( Four Over Six ): for each 16-element block, the quantizer tries scaling the block's maximum to 6 and to 4, and keeps whichever gives the lower reconstruction error (MAE). DSpark speculator with an RNN head. The checkpoint also ships a DSpark draft in place of Inkling's 8 chained MTP heads. The speculator has 5 layers and drafts 7 tokens per step. The head is the RNN variant that DeepSeek's DSpark paper described. Kernel fusion and PDL. vLLM aggressively fuses the collective communication and memory-bound ops between sublayers into a single kernel. With attention residuals, each boundary needs an all-reduce, a short convolution, a residual update, the attention-residual mix and an RMSNorm: five memory-bound steps on the same hidden states. The fused kernel, allreduce_conv_mix (gold in Figure 2), runs the all-reduce over NVLink multicast and keeps everything after it in registers. The GEMM, attention, routing and activation kernels launch with programmatic dependent launch (PDL), so each one's prologue overlaps the tail of the previous kernel, which matters at small batch sizes, where a decode step is a long chain of short kernels. items.title: LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B
items.story_key: story|ver:4.1|title:llmon an llm native markup language now in granite 4 1 3b and 8b
items.content_excerpt: LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections. To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages. Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview . We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates. JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans. LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. items.title: aws-emulator
items.summary:
aws-emulator

Finally, an official emulator from AWS to run tests against a local clone of their many different services without having to provision a paid API key to do so.

It's written in Rust by a huge swarm of agents - 29,684 commits in the first three weeks of the project. Swaminathan (Swami) Sivasubramanian wrote about how it came to be in a guest post on Werner Vogels' blog.

It currently requires Docker to run on macOS or Windows. I'm hoping they fix that in the future - it would be great if you could download a single binary and use that as part of a standard test suite in other languages and on other platforms.

items.title: claude-code v2.1.323
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added Code Mode, an experimental opt-in in which Claude writes JavaScript to call its tools; see https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-mode to turn it on, or to turn it off for an organization
  • Added engines["claude-code"] to plugin.json: plugins outside their stated Claude Code version range are not installed, updated or loaded, and install and update pick the newest version that fits
  • Added type checking of a plugin's TypeScript hooks module to claude plugin validate; each finding is a warning, and --strict fails on it
  • Added to claude plugin validate the $ nouns a mod's engine.create hook adds, withholds or replaces
  • Added support for CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_MODEL in managed settings for Claude Desktop sessions on third-party providers (takes effect once Claude Desktop includes this version)
  • Added an options menu (stop, switch to usage credits, upgrade) when a model needs usage credits that are turned off or used up
  • Added a progress heartbeat every 30 seconds while hooks run long in claude -p and SDK sessions, so a host such as Claude Desktop won't end the turn as hung (once it includes this version)
  • Added .docx support to Artifact tool asset uploads
  • Added a /diff to close hint to the diff panel, and the keys that focus and close a panel to the ? shortcut guide
  • Added a start-up warning for Bash allow rules with a * in a variable's value, such as Bash(PORT=* npm run dev)
  • Added a warning when a plugin's language server can't start, naming the server and what to check
  • Added a one-time startup notice naming CLAUDE_CODE_PERFORCE_MODE when Perforce settings are found and the mode is off
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES (available since 2.1.318): set it to 1 to turn off subagent progress summaries and the requests that write them (#86879)
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_HINT_COMMAND, which a program that starts Claude Code can set to have the exit hint name its own resume command
  • Added unsetOptionCount to the claude plugin install --json result: how many userConfig options are not yet set
  • Added isPromptCovered to the props a mod's pane is drawn with, telling it when a dialog or a field above the prompt covers the prompt
  • Fixed running /compact again, or after a command such as /context, summarizing away a message that Claude had not answered yet
  • Fixed a resumed session joining your next message to an old interrupted message that was not resumed
  • Fixed a memory spike at the next prompt after Claude changed a very large file
  • Fixed a setting saved in a running session undoing a hand edit made to settings.json moments earlier; a settings file you delete during a session now stays deleted
  • Fixed claude plugin commands and claude mcp list signing you out of a Console profile when they ended while the token was being renewed
  • Fixed Edit and Bash running out of memory on certain /proc files, and Edit hanging or running out of memory on devices and named pipes
  • Fixed Claude Code failing to start, or to clear stored credentials at sign-out, when saving its configuration file failed with "Out of memory"
  • Fixed requests sent without streaming failing on errors that streamed requests recover from, such as a rejected image, thinking block or beta header
  • Fixed ExitWorktree, the worktree exit dialog and /resume leaving the session in the wrong folder when the folder the shell was in before entering the worktree had been deleted
  • Fixed accents and other combining marks sometimes landing left of the text, leaving stale copies on screen, or silently disappearing when text wraps
  • Fixed the last key of a key chord, such as Enter in ctrl+x enter, acting on a dialog's text field when the chord's own action isn't available there
  • Fixed ps processes piling up when the process listing Claude Code runs before stopping a command takes too long
  • Fixed subagent transcripts and large tool results being saved apart from the session's transcript after entering a worktree created by a WorktreeCreate hook or belonging to a nested repository
  • Fixed a session on a named Anthropic profile moving to another sign-in when /fork, the Left arrow or --bg continued it in the background; reopen any session that was open during the update
  • Fixed a background session sending a conversation under another sign-in when its named Anthropic profile is missing, changed or overridden; it now stops and says so
  • Fixed a session on an API key, auth token or workload identity from its shell (not a setup token) moving to another sign-in in the background; it now stops and says so
  • Fixed MCP tool calls ending in the sign-in server's error, such as TOKEN_EXPIRED, instead of asking you to sign in again
  • Fixed an expired claude.ai login showing "Credit balance too low" when a saved Console key or ant auth login profile without credit was used instead
  • Fixed a session on a named Anthropic profile being handed to an older background service that could not keep its sign-in; it now says to restart the service
  • Fixed a background session's sign-in leaving the previous account's login or other credentials in place; it now clears them for every session on the computer, and a refused sign-in can leave no login
  • Fixed background sessions moving between a profile and the stored login when an update restarted them
  • Fixed sessions opened before a sign-in keeping signed-out feature flags after the sign-in
  • Fixed sessions that kept failing after a Claude apps gateway sign-in expired: once you sign in again with /login in another terminal, they carry on at the next message
  • Fixed the billing notice naming your ant auth login organization when a custom X-Api-Key header is set
  • macOS: Fixed "Not logged in · Please run /login" coming back right after a successful /login or a token refresh when the keychain was slow to answer
  • Fixed turns failing in Claude Desktop when an organization's gateway answers an expired token with 403: Claude Code now asks Desktop for a fresh token and retries
  • Fixed the error shown when Amazon Bedrock refuses your account a model: it no longer says to refresh your AWS credentials, it says to enable the model
  • Fixed the awsAuthRefresh or gcpAuthRefresh command sometimes running twice for one request when three or more sessions needed a fresh sign-in at once
  • Fixed the claude -p warning about an ended claude.ai login to say that claude auth logout also removes saved MCP server logins and plugin secrets
  • Fixed Bash permission prompts offering "don't ask again" for commands that write to sensitive paths such as .git or .claude, where the saved rule did not stop the next prompt
  • Fixed a case where some lsof commands ran without a permission prompt

items.content_excerpt: AI agents can multiply your query volume. Lakehouse//RT keeps your bill from multiplying with it. AI agents are pushing the limits of data warehouses. A human analyst might run a few dozen queries in an afternoon. An agent can run hundreds per second, around the clock. And with growing demand for use cases like customer-facing dashboards that refresh in milliseconds and applications with embedded analytics, real-time workloads are quickly becoming a standard part of how businesses use data. Most data warehouses were designed for human-scale query volume, not the sustained concurrency agents generate. And even when a warehouse can deliver low latency, the bill grows as fast as demand: 10x the queries could easily mean 10x the cost. We built Lakehouse//RT not only to serve real-time workloads directly on the lakehouse , but to do so without growing your costs at the same rate as your queries. Most data warehouses scale capacity in step with demand: more queries, more compute, more cost. That works well for many analytics workloads, where query volume tracks the number of people asking questions. Real-time workloads are different. When AI agents and thousands of concurrent users all need answers in milliseconds, query volume can grow far faster than headcount, and cost grows with it. Real-time workloads are also often spiky. The usual way to handle that is to overprovision: add capacity in large blocks and keep it running so latency holds up at peak. You end up paying for idle compute most of the day. Lakehouse//RT flips the equation. Instead of scaling cost with demand, it scales efficiency. Its engine is architected to serve dramatically more queries on the same resources, so when demand doubles (or increases tenfold), your infrastructure keeps pace without a proportional spike in spend. Organizations will not be able to outspend the demand curve. The only sustainable path is a system that does more per unit of compute. Concurrency is where real-time costs usually grow fastest. Traditional warehouses can only run so many queries at once; the rest wait in line or trigger more capacity. Serving hundreds of agents then means running several clusters just to keep response times steady. That's true even when most of those queries are small lookups that don't need the horsepower. items.title: FERN: Cross-Benchmark Table Retrieval for Text-to-SQL with Frozen Retrievers and Learned Ranking
items.summary: Text-to-SQL systems over large pooled catalogs must first retrieve the tables a question needs. We compare against the published table recall of RASL, which uses Claude 3.5 models to extract keywords and select tables, on pooled BIRD, Spider, and Fiben catalogs. FERN (Feature-Engineered Ranking with No generative LLM) instead fuses three frozen retrievers into 100 candidates, describes each with up to 120 features, and reorders them with LightGBM rankers fitted once on BIRD's training questions. On Spider, where it was not fitted, its candidate pool alone reaches RASL's published recall at fifteen tables (98.0), and the ranker raises the share of questions with every gold table in the top five (complete@5) from 83.9% to 95.6%. At five tables, FERN's recall is within one point of RASL's on Spider (96.7 vs 97.0) and on BIRD with its evidence hints (96.6 vs 97.5), and 8.2 points below on BIRD without them (89.3). On 121 real BEAVER questions, without BEAVER fitting, its recall at fifteen (82.1) falls between two BEAVER-trained retrievers (80.8, 84.5), but its complete@15 is below both (49.6 vs 54.5 and 62.0). On Fiben, it falls far short at fifteen tables (54.2 vs 69.2, different question sets), although its recall at fifty is numerically close to RASL's question-only retrieval result (80.7 vs 79.4). On BIRD dev with evidence, non-retrieval features raise complete@5 by 7.7 points over retrieval signals alone. On BIRD dev, median latency is 208 ms per question on one A100, without hosted model calls.

items.title: Mitigating Agentic Deception via Evaluation-Side Partially Observable Games
items.summary: As large language models become more capable agents, they can exhibit deceptive behaviors, cheating human for higher rewards while appearing helpful. We attribute this failure to evaluation-side partial observability, where models are evaluated mainly from final outcome, without checking the faithfulness of underlying reasoning, tool use, and environmental effects. Prior mitigations address this partial observability by predefined evaluator latent belief space or one-shot monitoring, which do not extend to free-form language space and vulnerable to stronger deceptions that evade simple monitoring. In this work, we formulate deception mitigation as an Evaluation-Side Partially Observable Extensive Form Game (e-PoG), a max-min framework in which an agent maximizes reward, a monitor minimizes the agent's payoff by exposing deception from the full interaction trajectory, and a fixed verifier validates the monitor's claims and converts them into penalties. We define the solution concept as a Subgame-Perfect Oversight Equilibrium (SPOE) between agent and monitor, and prove its existence in finite games. With a perfect verifier, every SPOE is faithful; with an imperfect verifier, the guarantee persists if verifier errors do not reverse the ranking of monitor actions. To achieve faithful SPOE, we derive a two-timescale policy gradient algorithm and enhance the pipeline empirically with NLI verification and deterministic checks. Experiments with Gemma3-4B-IT and Qwen3-4B/8B on Agentic Role-Playing, SearchQA, and WebShop show that e-PoG mitigates multiple emergent deception modes, outperforming the strongest baselines by 26.0% in deception mitigation and by up to 39.8% in task success. These gains persist under weak-to-strong supervision. Code is available at https://github.com/Toyoid/deceptive-agent.

items.title: LM-SimBench: A Unified Framework, Dataset, and Benchmark for Large Language Model Training Simulation
items.summary: Evaluating candidate parallelization strategies through distributed training runs makes strategy selection prohibitively expensive at scale. Performance simulation offers a lower cost alternative, yet controlled comparisons among existing simulators remain difficult because they differ in the training stages they model and the workloads on which they are evaluated. We introduce LM-SimBench, a unified framework, profiling dataset, and benchmark for evaluating LLM training simulators. The framework decomposes simulation into functional stages from model compilation to schedule level aggregation, connecting execution representations and cost estimators to measurable evaluation targets. Following this framework, we profile 23 model settings from 10 dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM families on an Ascend Neural Processing Unit (NPU) cluster. The resulting dataset contains 348 feasible configurations that jointly vary five parallelism dimensions and activation recomputation, with six views spanning configuration, rank, operator, event, and kernel granularity. Evaluations of representative training simulators demonstrate how LM-SimBench supports comparisons of prediction accuracy, assessment of configuration selection, and diagnosis of prediction errors. Matched GPU-NPU experiments validate the cross-platform applicability of the collection and evaluation protocol and demonstrate NPU-guided GPU configuration selection.

items.title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime
items.summary: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. No harness-based method gains on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.

items.content_excerpt: How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signal’s cryptographic protocol — long considered to be a grand security challenge Today, we’re sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verification—mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws—is the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive. Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI. AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human – just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them. But most protocol verification stops at the design level.
